notes.b: Green plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, using light energy. This process is photosynthesis.
points: Word equation: carbon dioxide + water, in the presence of light and chlorophyll, gives glucose + oxygen.
Chlorophyll, the green pigment in the chloroplasts of leaf cells, absorbs light energy and uses it to drive the reaction.
Diagram: leaf cross-section labelled with stomata, palisade cells containing chloroplasts, and arrows showing carbon dioxide entering and oxygen leaving.

notes.h: Getting the raw materials to the leaf
points: Carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaf through stomata, small pores mainly on the lower surface.
Root hair cells absorb water, which is carried up the stem to the leaves in the xylem.
Oxygen, the by-product of photosynthesis, diffuses out of the leaf through the stomata.

notes.h: What the plant does with its glucose
points: Glucose is used in respiration, releasing energy for growth and the plant's other processes.
Surplus glucose is joined into starch, an insoluble store kept in leaves, stems, roots and tubers such as potatoes.
Glucose is converted to sucrose, which is carried in the phloem to other parts of the plant.
Glucose is joined into cellulose, the main structural material of plant cell walls.
Plants are producers: people and animals obtain their carbohydrates by eating plants, or animals that have eaten plants.
The sugars, starch and fibre in the diet all trace back to photosynthesis.
Photosynthesis releases the oxygen that the body uses in aerobic respiration.

keyTerms.definition: The process by which green plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen.
The green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
The organelle in leaf cells that contains chlorophyll and is the site of photosynthesis.
Small pores, mainly on the underside of a leaf, through which carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves.
An organism, such as a green plant, that makes its own food from simple substances.
The plant tissue that carries water and mineral salts up from the roots to the leaves.
The plant tissue that transports sucrose and other dissolved food from the leaves to the rest of the plant.
An insoluble polysaccharide that plants store in leaves, stems, roots and tubers as an energy reserve.

factCards.definition: Light energy, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide and water.
Glucose, which the plant uses or stores, and oxygen, which is released.

factCards.term: Three things a plant does with surplus glucose
factCards.definition: Converts it to starch for storage, to cellulose for cell walls, or to sucrose for transport.

factCards.term: Two gases exchanged through the stomata
factCards.definition: Carbon dioxide enters the leaf and oxygen leaves it.

factCards.term: Route taken by water in a plant
factCards.definition: From the roots, up the stem to the leaves, through the xylem.

questions.prompt: Explain how a green plant converts carbon dioxide and water into glucose, naming the energy source and the gas released.
questions.model: Light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll in the chloroplasts. Carbon dioxide enters the leaf through the stomata and water is absorbed by the roots and carried to the leaves in the xylem. The reaction produces glucose, and oxygen is released as a by-product through the stomata.

questions.prompt: Trace the route of carbohydrate from its formation in a leaf to its storage and use within the plant, and explain why photosynthesis matters to people.
questions.model: Glucose is formed in the chloroplasts of leaf cells by photosynthesis. The plant uses some glucose in respiration to release energy for growth. Surplus glucose is joined into starch and stored in leaves, stems, roots and tubers. Glucose is converted to sucrose and transported in the phloem to other parts of the plant. Glucose is also joined into cellulose to build cell walls. People depend on photosynthesis because plants are producers: all dietary carbohydrate comes directly from plants or from animals that eat plants. Photosynthesis also releases the oxygen needed for aerobic respiration.
